BTW Buildathon 2026, Track 2. The Noon Curveball has landed. You are the FRESH session the rules require — reconstruct from Checkpoint context, do not assume you know this codebase.

CONFIRM FIRST, STOP IF ANY FAILS
  pwd                        -> /Users/adharsh/git/BTW-buildathon/entire-graph
  git branch --show-current  -> pivot-work-order
  entire session current     -> must NAME a session, not "No active session found"
  git remote -v              -> entire://aws-ap-south-1.entire.io/gh/adharshd/entire-graph

WHERE THINGS STAND
Last stable pre-curveball commit: 90d1939, Entire checkpoint 9ab0f807a913, pushed, remote in sync.
`main` is PROTECTED on the mirror and a push to it is rejected — all work stays on pivot-work-order.
Do not rewrite history: two early commits (abbf061, 4a0a219) carry no checkpoint, and backfilling
them would break the ten that work.

STEP 1 — RECONSTRUCT FROM CHECKPOINT (graded — do this before reading anything else)
  entire checkpoint list
  entire checkpoint show 9ab0f807a913      # if that verb is wrong: entire checkpoint --help
  git show 90d1939 --stat                  # its message carries intent/architecture/completed/open risks

THEN READ, IN THIS ORDER
  docs/ENTIRE-TIPS.md            <- START HERE. Part 1 is the exact command sequence for this
                                    curveball, step by step. Part 2 is 14 navigation gotchas
                                    already paid for today (checkpoint traps, protected main,
                                    two-agents-one-worktree rules, test gotchas).
  docs/POST-CURVEBALL-PLAN.md    the plan written before the constraint landed
  BUILDATHON.md                  problem, architecture, verified findings
  docs/demo/                     graph evidence + the mux verification loop already captured

THE TRACK 2 CARD
"Graph is evidence, not an oracle." Requirements: must not present incomplete graph relationships as
certain; must identify when analysis may be partial; must provide a safe fallback or verification
path; existing behaviour for fully resolved code must keep working; must include a test or fixture
representing incomplete analysis; use Entire Graph to identify which parts of the implementation
consume relationship/impact/semantic-diff evidence. Users AND agents must be able to tell apart:
confirmed structural evidence / heuristic or incomplete evidence / claims needing source or test
verification. A partial-analysis fixture is attached — get it from the organisers, do not invent one.

THE TRAP — READ THIS TWICE
PivotMap's existing thesis is already "graph is evidence, not an oracle": it has UNREACHED, it prints
"SAFE means no path found", it ships known_blind_spots. The tempting response is "we already did
this." That scores in the PARTIAL band, because the rubric wants a clear statement of which
assumption the curveball INVALIDATED. Claiming nothing changed means no adaptation to score.

THE ASSUMPTION THAT WAS ACTUALLY INVALIDATED (verify this, do not take it on trust)
Uncertainty is tiered at the LANGUAGE level (semantic vs inventory-only) but NOT at the EDGE level.
Inside Go these two are rendered identically and treated identically by the classifier:
    IMPORTS os/exec         confidence 1.00   <- a fact
    CALLS   regexp.go       confidence 0.68   <- "matched globally unique method name", a heuristic
A P0 work item can rest entirely on the second, and nothing says so. Confidence is carried through
the whole pipeline and never used to affect a verdict, a priority, an action, or the plan.

STRONGEST SUSPECTED FINDING — CONFIRM IT IN SOURCE FIRST
buildPivotResponse (internal/cli/pivot.go) copies snapshot.Header.Warnings and
snapshot.Header.PartialFailures into the response but appears never to consult them when assigning a
verdict. Meanwhile `entire graph impact` self-reports "Completeness: degraded for Go" with
W_DATA_FLOW_EVIDENCE_UNMERGED. If that holds, SAFE currently conflates "fully parsed, no path found"
with "the parser had diagnostics here, and no path found" — which is exactly the distinction the card
demands. Verify against source before claiming it.

PROPOSED REVISION — focused, preserves existing behaviour
Three evidence tiers, surfaced to BOTH audiences (the card says "users and agents"):
    CONFIRMED   import/declaration edges, high confidence, clean parse        -> trust
    HEURISTIC   name-matched calls, low confidence                            -> verify against source
    UNVERIFIED  file had parse warnings or partial failures                   -> cannot be SAFE
  - text output tags each evidence line with its tier
  - plan JSON gains evidence_quality per work item and verification_required
  - execution_contract.must_not_claim gains a clause forbidding an agent from treating a heuristic
    edge as fact
  - fully-resolved code must behave EXACTLY as before — that is the "preserve existing behaviour"
    requirement and what keeps this a focused revision rather than a rewrite

SCORING CONSTRAINTS — these decide the 15 points
  - "Graph use that happens AFTER implementation, or an explanation given verbally rather than
    captured in context, scores in the partial band." So: run every graph command BEFORE the first
    edit, and pipe each one to a file under docs/demo/curveball/ so it is captured, not spoken.
  - Run `entire graph impact` before editing. Save the output.
  - Dogfood it: `entire graph pivot --repo . --dependency internal/sem --exclude-tests --depth 1
    --format plan` should name your own evidence consumers. UNVERIFIED — if it returns zero
    invalidated files the matcher did not resolve an internal package path; fall back to search and
    impact, and record that as a finding rather than reporting an empty result.
  - Tests are required for the new behaviour, plus a fixture for incomplete analysis.
  - Final commit message must state: what assumption changed, how the design changed, why the new
    result is safe. That message becomes the final Checkpoint.

TESTING NOTES
  go build ./... && go test ./internal/cli/ -count=1     # ~55-75s
  If a colour assertion fails, re-run with `env -u FORCE_COLOR` before believing you broke it.
  cmd/graph-bench fails on this machine (local git rejects `checkout --end-of-options`) — pre-existing,
  unrelated. Never claim a fully green suite; name the condition.
  Before believing any failure is yours: git stash your changes, re-run, unstash.

HOW I WANT YOU TO WORK
  - Commit after each meaningful step; every commit must carry an Entire checkpoint. Verify with
    `git log --format="%(trailers:key=Entire-Checkpoint,valueonly)" -1`, never assume.
  - `git pull --rebase origin pivot-work-order` before committing; stage by explicit path, never -A.
    A second agent session may be working in this same worktree.
  - Graph output is evidence, not an oracle — read the cited source before acting on it. That is
    literally this track's theme, so behave accordingly.
  - Explain changes to me in plain language as you go; I must be able to defend the code myself.
  - A smaller working thing beats an ambitious broken one. If time runs short, stop and commit.
  - Never report that tests pass without having run them.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai IndMoney

You are a multilingual financial portfolio and investing assistant for INDmoney, helping users
analyze their full portfolio across asset classes and answer market, stock, and derivatives questions.

INDmoney context (always):
  - When giving context, explanations, or next steps — especially for generic asks like "I want to buy",
    "how do I invest", "where should I start", or "add money" — frame everything in terms of INDmoney:
    the INDmoney app, their linked accounts, watchlist, SIPs, and portfolio tools available here.
  - Do not name, suggest, or compare other brokers, trading apps, or competitor platforms unless the
    user explicitly asks about them or names one first.

CAPABILITIES:
  - Full portfolio analysis: Indian stocks, mutual funds, bonds, EPF, NPS, US stocks, and other assets
  - Allocation, diversification, sector exposure, concentration, and portfolio quality
  - Indian stocks, indices, and F&O analysis: price action, candlestick patterns, support/resistance, breakouts
  - Market summaries: index direction, top movers, unusual volume, sector and derivatives signals
  - Technical analysis for intraday/swing/trading; fundamental analysis for long-term/portfolio decisions

TOOL ROUTING:

2. Tool Usage Rules:
   Resolution:
   - Always call lookup_ind_keys first to resolve any stock, index, derivative, or mutual fund name to an ind_key. Never assume or guess an ind_key.
   - For MCX commodities — gold, silver, crude oil, natural gas, copper, zinc, aluminium, nickel and
     their mini/micro variants — call lookup_ind_keys with filter_type="IN_COMMODITY". IN_STOCKS_FNO
     covers equity and index derivatives ONLY and returns unrelated equity options for a commodity
     name, so never use it for these. The lookup returns the futures contract; pass that key to
     get_indian_stocks_option_chain, get_indian_stocks_details or get_indian_stocks_ohlc.

  Net worth and portfolio:
   - Use networth_snapshot for total net worth, full allocation breakdown, liabilities, or any broad financial summary.

- bdd-gherkin: Generate BDD Gherkin feature files from requirements — even vague ones. This skill collaborates with the user by asking targeted clarifying questions to uncover hidden assumptions, edge cases, and acceptance criteria, then produces well-structured Given/When/Then scenarios. No source code needed. Use this skill whenever the user asks to write BDD requirements, Gherkin scenarios, .feature files, acceptance criteria in Given/When/Then format, or behavior-driven test specifications. Also trigger when the user mentions "BDD", "Gherkin", "Cucumber", "feature file", "acceptance tests", or "Given/When/Then" in the context of writing requirements or test scenarios.
- build-knowledge-base: Turn a list of research links (typically the output of the /research-prompt skill pasted back from Google AI Mode / Perplexity / ChatGPT) into a topic-organized knowledge base of FULL VERBATIM source content. Fetches complete blog/article text and full video/podcast transcripts, saves each source as its own markdown file, organizes them by TOPIC (not media type), and writes a taught _overview.md synthesis per topic plus a README index. Uses curl + trafilatura for articles, a reader proxy for bot-blocked/JS pages, and youtube-transcript-api for videos. Invoke with /build-knowledge-base <topic> and paste/point to the link list.
- celebrate-progress: Celebrate the completion of a task, PR, or milestone! Generates a fun, energetic celebration message inspired by "DJ Got Us Fallin' in Love" by Usher. Use when work is done and approved — this is the victory lap.
- commit-push: Stage, commit, and push changes to the remote repository. Analyzes the current diff, generates a commit message, confirms it with the user before committing, then pushes. Use this skill whenever the user says "commit and push", "commit-push", "ship it", "push my changes", or invokes /commit-push.
- commit-push-pr: Stage, commit, push, and open a pull request in one workflow. Confirms commit message, PR title, and description before acting. Use when the user says "commit push and PR", "push and raise a PR", or invokes /commit-push-pr.
- conventions-check: Check code changes against project conventions. Supports two modes: a PR number (e.g., `/conventions-check 863`) to analyze a PR diff, or file paths/globs (e.g., `/conventions-check src/**/*.java`) to check specific files. Discovers conventions from the project's own codebase (CLAUDE.md, linter configs, existing patterns) and reports violations in naming, patterns, architecture, and file organization. Use this skill whenever someone asks to "check conventions", "review code style", "audit patterns", or "validate naming".
- discussion-blackboard: Run a multi-agent adversarial discussion on a hard design or debug problem. Spawns N persistent Claude subagents and rotates them through postures (Adversary / Proposer / Synthesizer / Boundary Expert), each turn expressed as one Typed Move (ATTACK / EXTEND / BOUND / VERIFY / PASS-WITH-JUSTIFICATION) on a shared `blackboard.md`. The lead Claude orchestrates: assigns turns, validates moves, rejects malformed ones, and terminates when the Adversary passes with justification AND all CRITICAL claims are verified, OR a 12-turn cap fires. Ships a read-only HTML viewer so the human can follow the (very fast) thought process. Use for hard architecture decisions, design reviews where you want adversarial pressure, or weed-level debugging where one agent isn't enough. This is the v2 of `discuss-with-codex` — both skills coexist; use this one when you want a full panel rather than a 1-on-1 second opinion.
- generate-endpoint: generate-endpoint
- get-api-docs: Use this skill to get documentation for third-party APIs, SDKs or libraries before writing code that uses them to ensure you have the latest, most accurate documentation. This is a better way to find documentation than doing web search. This includes when a user asks for tasks like "use the OpenAI API", "call the Stripe API", "use the Anthropic SDK", "query Pinecone", or any other time the user asks you to write code against an external service and you need current API reference.  Fetch the docs with chub before answering, rather than relying on your pre-trained knowledge, which may be outdated because of recent changes to these APIs. Be sure to use this skill when the user asks for the latest docs, latest API behavior, or explicitly mentions chub or Context Hub. Ensure `chub` is available, run `chub --help`, then follow the instructions there.
- give-me-a-commit-message: Suggest 4-6 single-line commit message options based on the current staged and unstaged changes. Each option is single-line (no newlines) but may contain multiple sentences. Each option comes with a one-line "what this option emphasizes" explainer so the user can choose based on what story they want the commit to tell. Does NOT commit or push — just outputs options for the user to copy. Extracts ticket ID from the current branch name if present. Invoke with /give-me-a-commit-message.
- grill-me: Interview the user relentlessly about a plan or design until reaching shared understanding, resolving each branch of the decision tree. Use when user wants to stress-test a plan, get grilled on their design, or mentions "grill me".
- grill-me-externally: Generate a comprehensive, anonymized grilling session of recent code changes — ready to paste into an external AI (Gemini, ChatGPT, Perplexity). Combines the depth of /grill-me with the privacy-safety of /anonymize-prompt. Use when the user wants a tough external review of a change set. Triggered by /grill-me-externally, "grill me externally", "anonymous grilling", "ask Gemini to grill my changes", or similar. Output is one or more pastable prompts; every proprietary detail is anonymized first.
- html-it: Convert a markdown document (plan, design doc, alignment doc, review notes) into a rich, standalone HTML file with embedded CSS — light theme, system fonts, card-based sections, GitHub-ish color palette. Inspired by the Claude blog post on the unreasonable effectiveness of HTML. The goal is a self-contained .html the reader opens in a browser instead of squinting at a wall of markdown. Invoke with /html-it [path-to-md]. If no path is given, defaults to the most recently modified .md in ~/.claude/plans/ or the current working directory.
- prompt-claude-design: Generate a focused, context-rich prompt for Claude Design (Anthropic's browser-based UI design product) by reading the current implementation plan AND the most recent Claude Design handoff bundle in the repo. Outputs a copy-paste-ready prompt that grounds Claude Design in what's already been decided, so the next design iteration moves the work forward instead of re-litigating prior choices. No anonymization — Claude Design is an Anthropic product. Triggered by /prompt-claude-design or when the user says "ask Claude Design", "prompt Claude Design", "next round with Claude Design", or "send to Claude Design".
- research-prompt: Generate a copy-paste research prompt for an external AI (Google AI Mode, Perplexity, ChatGPT, etc.) that returns a categorized knowledge base of the best resources on a topic: primary/original sources, official documentation, in-depth analysis blogs, videos/talks, academic papers, and tools. The output is a single self-contained prompt block the user can paste directly into Google AI Mode to gather authoritative links. Invoke with /research-prompt <topic>. Optionally add focus notes after the topic.
- ship: Ship your staged changes: runs a conventions check on staged files, generates a commit message with ticket ID from branch name, commits, and pushes. Use this instead of manual git commit + push. Invoke with `/ship` or when the user says "ship it", "commit and push", or "send it".
- work-towards-alignment: Run a collaborative session that actively works toward user–Claude alignment on a plan, design, or PR review. Bidirectional and user-paced — Claude first probes the user's foundational knowledge in chat (teaching where needed), THEN writes the alignment doc reflecting what was learned, THEN walks through each claim with the foundation already in place. Tracks state in docs/<topic>-alignment.md. Use when the user says "align me", "work towards alignment", "make sure we're on the same page about <plan>", "I need to understand this before approving", or invokes /work-towards-alignment.
- work-towards-alignment-simple: Markdown-only alignment skill. Two-phase collaborative session — probe foundational knowledge first, then walk claims one by one until the user explicitly signals alignment. All output is plain .md. Invoke with /work-towards-alignment-simple <path-to-plan-or-topic>.
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo).     docs: last stable state before the Noon Curveball
    
    Preserves the pre-curveball snapshot so a fresh session can reconstruct this work
    without inheriting the current agent's memory. Everything a successor needs to resume
    is in these four files plus BUILDATHON.md.
    
    INTENT
    PivotMap answers what survives a requirement that changed after the code was written.
    Given a prohibited dependency it splits the tree into INVALIDATED (a graph edge reaches
    the dependency), AT-RISK (reachable from an invalidated file, breadth-first, capped),
    SAFE (no path found) and UNREACHED (inventory-only language, so genuinely unknown).
    Every verdict prints the edge that produced it, so a reader checks the claim rather
    than trusting it.
    
    ARCHITECTURE
    internal/cli/pivot.go        classifier, flags, BFS propagation, JSON response
    internal/cli/pivot_roles.go  file roles + the grouped text renderer
    internal/cli/pivot_plan.go   pivot-plan/v1 work order emitter (--format plan)
    Registered in root.go and help.go; TestRegistryMatchesDispatch enforces parity.
    No model produces a verdict. The interpretive step -- a sentence becoming a package
    name -- stays outside the binary, which is what keeps doctor's no_egress=true honest.
    
    COMPLETED
    - Roles (PRODUCTION/TEST/TEST_FIXTURE/GENERATED/VENDOR/UNKNOWN) rank and group the
      report and never change a verdict.
    - --format plan binds work to `action`, not `verdict`, so an agent does not treat every
      reachable file as an edit target.
    - The verification loop ran end to end on gorilla/mux with --dependency bytes:
      1 invalidated -> 0, executed by an agent with no prior context, then re-measured by
      re-running the same rules. The count alone is not the evidence, because deletion
      satisfies it equally: the diff was 1 file, +7/-8, no test touched, suite green
      before and after.

      ambient FORCE_COLOR, and an unreproducible plan id printed in BUILDATHON.md.

      the branch explicitly is the highest-value item left.

    - SAFE means no path found in one snapshot, never proof of absence.

# Entire tips

Two halves: the exact commands the Noon Curveball asks for, then the navigation
gotchas already paid for in this repository. Everything here was hit for real, not
read from a manual.

# Part 1 — curveball commands, in order

Track 2: *Graph is evidence, not an oracle.* Every command below maps to a line the
card or the scoring rubric actually asks for. Run them in this order.

> Scoring warning, verbatim: **"Graph use that happens after implementation, or an
> explanation given verbally rather than captured in context, scores in the partial
> band."** Every graph command here runs **before** the first edit, and its output gets
> saved to a file so it is captured in context rather than spoken.

---

## Step 0 — before ending this session

Card: *"Commit your last stable version. Confirm Entire created a Checkpoint."*

```sh
git add <explicit paths>
git commit                       # message should carry intent, architecture, done, open risks
entire status                    # must say: Enabled · branch <name> · checkpoints sync to origin
git log --format="%h %s%n  ckpt: %(trailers:key=Entire-Checkpoint,valueonly)" -1
git push origin pivot-work-order # this also pushes refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1
```

Done already: `90d1939`, checkpoint `9ab0f807a913`, pushed.

Then end the session.

---

## Step 1 — fresh session, reconstruct from checkpoint

# Part 2 — navigation gotchas


## 1. The checkpoint trap — check this before anything else

Entire's hooks live in `.claude/settings.json` and load **only if the agent session was
launched from inside that directory**. Launch from the parent folder and you get commits
with no checkpoints — silently. `entire doctor` reports green the whole time, because it
inspects the repo's settings file and cannot see where the agent was started from.

Two commits in this repo (`abbf061`, `4a0a219`) have no checkpoint for exactly this reason.

```sh
pwd                     # must be the repo root that holds .claude/settings.json
entire session current  # must NAME a session, not "No active session found"
entire checkpoint list  # after your first commit, must be > 0
```

**A green `doctor` is not proof.** The only proof is a checkpoint count that goes up
after a real commit.

## 2. Verify a checkpoint actually bound — do not assume

The trailer is on the commit itself, so read it from git rather than trusting a tool:

```sh
git log --format="%h %s%n  ckpt: %(trailers:key=Entire-Checkpoint,valueonly)" -1
```

Audit the whole branch at once:

```sh
git log <branch> ^origin/main --format="%h %s ckpt=%(trailers:key=Entire-Checkpoint,valueonly)"
```

## 3. `entire checkpoint list` is branch-scoped

It reports `branch <name>` and counts only that branch. Switch branches and the number
changes. That is not data loss — it is a filter. Confirm with `git ls-remote origin`,
which shows the real refs.

## 4. Checkpoints link by SHA, not by branch

Two consequences:

- **Fast-forwarding a branch into another name is safe.** No SHA moves, so nothing breaks.
- **Rewriting history is the thing that destroys them.** `--force`, amend, or rebase after
  push changes SHAs, and every checkpoint pointing at the old ones is orphaned.

Never run `entire session attach --force` on a pushed branch. It amends the last commit
to add a trailer — rewriting published history. Without `--force` the checkpoint is still
created and the trailer is printed for you to paste into a later commit.

**If two early commits lack checkpoints, leave them.** Backfilling breaks the ten that
work to fix the two that do not.

## 5. The checkpoint ref pushes with your branch

`refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1` is a separate ref carrying the checkpoint payload.
`git push origin <branch>` pushes it too — you will see:

```
[entire] Pushing entire/checkpoints/v1 to origin....... done
```

`entire status` tells you when one is pending:

> `1 checkpoint not yet on origin — it syncs with your next 'git push origin'`

## 6. `main` may be protected on the mirror

A direct push is rejected outright:

```
! [remote rejected] pivot-work-order -> main (protected branch)
```

Non-destructive — nothing changes locally. But **find out early, not at 2:55pm.**

Consequence for judging: the web UI's Overview page renders the **default branch**. If
`main` is stale, that page shows an old commit and "No checkpoint activity", which looks
catastrophic and is purely a display artefact. Check the real state:

```sh
git ls-remote origin
```

Then point people at the branch tree URL and the **Sessions** tab, never the repo root.

## 7. Your work may span more than one session

This conversation produced two Entire sessions (`35d4b996`, then `fea6b82a`), apparently
when the background job re-attached. Harmless — checkpoints bind to commits, not sessions
— but it means **checkpoint links are spread across several session pages**.

For submission, give the milestone → checkpoint → commit mapping explicitly rather than
linking one session:

```
1  initial understanding    bb0d72d79dbc -> 2ff8446
2  last stable before noon  9ab0f807a913 -> 90d1939
```

Also: session titles are derived from prompts. A throwaway prompt becomes the session
name a judge sees. Worth renaming before submission if the UI allows it.

## 8. Checkpoint prompts can cross-attribute between concurrent sessions

With two agent sessions in one worktree, a checkpoint created by session A was observed
carrying session B's prompt text. The **commit linkage is correct**; only the prompt
label is misleading. Know this before reading the checkpoint list as a narrative.

## 9. Two agents in one worktree — rules that actually work

- `git pull --rebase origin <branch>` **before** every commit.
- Stage by **explicit path**, never `git add -A`.
- Agree file lanes up front. Disjoint lanes cannot collide.
- Check `stat -f "%Sm" <file>` if you suspect someone is mid-edit — a file written 90
  seconds ago means the other session is live in it.
- A broken build mid-refactor is usually someone else working, not a bug to fix.

For a scratch worktree, adopt the session **before** the first commit or the commits
will not link:

```sh
entire session adopt <session-id> --from /path/to/primary/worktree
```

## 10. Graph commands worth knowing

```sh
entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "<the task in one sentence>"
entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X          # callers, callees, types, co-change
entire graph diff --base A --head B --json       # semantic diff
entire graph capabilities --json                 # which languages are semantic vs inventory-only
```

- Run `impact` **before** a risky change. After the edit it does not prove the same thing.
- `impact` self-reports `Completeness: degraded for Go` with warnings next to its answer.
  That is the tool naming its own incompleteness — show it, do not hide it.
- Results are **evidence, not an oracle**. Interface dispatch, reflection and generated
  code leave no edge. `impact --symbol Route.Match` on gorilla/mux reports 0 callers even
  though `Router.Match` calls it through an interface.

## 11. The standalone binary has no `graph` prefix

Through the plugin it is `entire graph pivot`. A binary built straight from
`./cmd/entire-graph` takes the subcommand directly:

```sh
go build -o /tmp/eg ./cmd/entire-graph    # needs CGO for tree-sitter
/tmp/eg pivot --repo . --dependency os/exec --format json    # NOT "/tmp/eg graph pivot"
```

Getting this wrong produces empty output and a confusing JSON parse error downstream.

## 12. Measure from a clean detached build, not the live tree

To reproduce numbers at an old commit without disturbing a worktree someone else is
using:

```sh
git worktree add --detach /path/to/scratch <commit>
cd /path/to/scratch && go build -o ./bin ./cmd/entire-graph
# ... measure ...
git worktree remove --force /path/to/scratch
```

Counts are **file counts**, so they drift as later commits add files. Label a table with
the commit it was measured at, or a judge re-running the command gets different numbers
and stops believing the page.

## 13. Test gotchas in this repo

- `cmd/graph-bench` fails locally: it clones from github and the local git rejects
  `checkout --end-of-options`. **Pre-existing.** Do not try to fix it; do not claim a
  fully green suite.
- `internal/cli` takes ~55-75s. Budget for it before committing.
- If a test fails on ANSI colour codes, check `FORCE_COLOR` in your environment. Some
  tests read ambient colour settings, so they pass in CI and fail on a developer machine.
  Confirm with `env -u FORCE_COLOR go test ./...` before believing you broke something.

## 14. Before you believe any failure is yours

```sh
git stash push -q <your files>
go test ./...            # does it fail at clean HEAD too?
git stash pop -q
```

Thirty seconds, and it separates "I broke it" from "it was already broken".

entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "<the task in one sentence>"
entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X          # callers, callees, types, co-change
entire graph diff --base A --head B --json       # semantic diff
entire graph capabilities --json                 # which languages are semantic vs inventory-only
```

- Run `impact` **before** a risky change. After the edit it does not prove the same thing.
- `impact` self-reports `Completeness: degraded for Go` with warnings next to its answer.
  That is the tool naming its own incompleteness — show it, do not hide it.
- Results are **evidence, not an oracle**. Interface dispatch, reflection and generated
  code leave no edge. `impact --symbol Route.Match` on gorilla/mux reports 0 callers even
  though `Router.Match` calls it through an interface.

## 11. The standalone binary has no `graph` prefix

Through the plugin it is `entire graph pivot`. A binary built straight from
`./cmd/entire-graph` takes the subcommand directly:

```sh
go build -o /tmp/eg ./cmd/entire-graph    # needs CGO for tree-sitter
/tmp/eg pivot --repo . --dependency os/exec --format json    # NOT "/tmp/eg graph pivot"
```

Getting this wrong produces empty output and a confusing JSON parse error downstream.

## 12. Measure from a clean detached build, not the live tree

To reproduce numbers at an old commit without disturbing a worktree someone else is
using:

```sh
git worktree add --detach /path/to/scratch <commit>
cd /path/to/scratch && go build -o ./bin ./cmd/entire-graph
# ... measure ...
git worktree remove --force /path/to/scratch
```

Counts are **file counts**, so they drift as later commits add files. Label a table with
the commit it was measured at, or a judge re-running the command gets different numbers
and stops believing the page.

## 13. Test gotchas in this repo

- `cmd/graph-bench` fails locally: it clones from github and the local git rejects
  `checkout --end-of-options`. **Pre-existing.** Do not try to fix it; do not claim a
  fully green suite.
- `internal/cli` takes ~55-75s. Budget for it before committing.
- If a test fails on ANSI colour codes, check `FORCE_COLOR` in your environment. Some
  tests read ambient colour settings, so they pass in CI and fail on a developer machine.
  Confirm with `env -u FORCE_COLOR go test ./...` before believing you broke something.

## 14. Before you believe any failure is yours

```sh
git stash push -q <your files>
go test ./...            # does it fail at clean HEAD too?
git stash pop -q
```

Thirty seconds, and it separates "I broke it" from "it was already broken".

# PivotMap

## One-sentence summary

`entire graph pivot` answers what survives a requirement that changed after the code was already
written: which files break the new rule, which ones are built on the files that break it, and which
ones can be left alone.

## Problem, intended user and why it matters

A constraint arrives after the work is done. A dependency may no longer touch customer data. An
architecture rule now forbids background workers. A vendor is dropped. The code is already written,
and the developer now has to answer three questions before touching anything:

1. Which code actually violates this?
2. What else breaks if I rip that out?
3. What can I safely leave alone?

Today that is manual archaeology. `git log` shows what changed but not why anyone chose it. Grep finds
the banned import but not the three modules quietly built on top of it. So the developer either
over-reworks — treating the whole area as suspect — or under-reworks and ships a break.

The user is a developer or a coding agent that has just been handed a changed requirement and needs a
defensible plan for what to keep, rework, and drop, in an order they can start executing immediately.

## Selected Entire track and why Entire is essential

**Track 2 — Build with Graph Intelligence.**

The two halves of this problem map onto Entire's two primitives, and neither half is answerable alone:

- **Entire Graph** knows what connects to what. Given a prohibited package it can name every file that
  imports it, and every file that depends on those, with a confidence score and a source line per edge.
  It cannot know why any of it was built.
- **Entire Checkpoints** know why. A checkpoint carries the session that produced a commit — the intent,
  the reasoning, what was rejected. It has no idea what depends on the result.

PivotMap is the join. Graph supplies the blast radius; a checkpoint supplies the intent behind the code
inside that radius and flags which of the affected files this session actually wrote. Remove Graph and
there is no propagation, only grep. Remove checkpoints and the report can still classify, but it loses
the "why was this built this way" that makes a rework plan trustworthy.

## Architecture and main workflow

One new command in this fork, in three files, registered in the existing dispatcher in
`internal/cli/root.go`:

- `internal/cli/pivot.go` — flags, graph load, the three classification rules, propagation, JSON.
- `internal/cli/pivot_roles.go` — file-role classification and the grouped text report.
- `internal/cli/pivot_plan.go` — the `pivot-plan/v1` work order.

```
entire graph pivot --dependency <prohibited package> [--checkpoint <id>] [--depth N]
                   [--exclude-tests] [--format text|json|plan]
```

Pipeline:

1. **Load the graph.** `sem.LoadOrBuildProviderSnapshot` — the same call `impact` uses, so pivot reuses
   the plugin's existing parse and cache rather than building a second index.
2. **Rule 1, direct conflict.** Any file with an `IMPORTS`, `CALLS`, or `CONSTRUCTS` edge reaching the
   prohibited dependency is **INVALIDATED**. This is checkpoint-independent by design: code written
   before Entire was ever enabled still violates a new constraint, and a classifier that could only see
   checkpointed files would silently clear all of it.
3. **Rule 2, propagation.** Breadth-first from the invalidated set over dependency edges. Anything
   reached is **AT-RISK**, recorded with its hop distance. Capped at 2 hops by default.
4. **Rule 3, the rest.** No path to anything invalidated means **SAFE** — but only for languages the
   graph parses semantically. Files in inventory-only languages are reported as **UNREACHED**, because
   calling a file safe when the parser never checked it for relations would be asserting an absence
   nobody verified.
5. **Checkpoint overlay (optional).** `sem.AnalyzeCheckpoint` folds in what a session changed and how
   many dependents each change has, and marks affected files that session wrote with `*`.
6. **Role pass.** Every file is classified **PRODUCTION | TEST | TEST_FIXTURE | GENERATED | VENDOR |
   UNKNOWN** from signals that cannot be argued with: a `vendor/` path segment, a
   `testdata|fixtures|mocks` segment, the `_test.go` suffix, or the `Code generated ... DO NOT EDIT.`
   header the generator itself wrote. The role never changes a verdict — it decides how the finished
   report is grouped and ranked.
7. **Render.** `text` for a person, `json` for the full classification, `plan` for an agent.

`--exclude-tests` (the same path predicate `impact` and `neighbors` use) drops test files *before*
classification rather than filtering them out of the finished report. The difference matters for
propagation, not just for the listing: a test file is not a foundation anything ships on, so a
production file whose only route to invalidated code runs through a test file should come back Safe,
not At-Risk. The count of excluded files is printed, because a file that was never classified is not
a file that came back Safe.

Every verdict prints the edge that produced it — relation type, target, confidence, source line — so a
reader can check the claim rather than trust it.

### Three design decisions worth defending

**The classifier is rules, not a model.** No LLM produces a verdict. The interpretive step — turning a
sentence like "we can't send customer data through Library X" into the package name `libraryx` — stays
outside this binary, and `--dependency` takes the result directly. That is not only a design
preference: `entire graph doctor` asserts `no_egress=true`, and a model call inside the plugin would
make the plugin's own diagnostic lie.

**Propagation is capped.** Unbounded transitive closure marks an entire repository At-Risk, which is
technically true and completely useless. Two hops, with the distance reported per file, keeps the
output a shortlist a person can actually work through.

**Roles rank the report; they never filter it.** The first version of this tool had a real usability
bug, and it was not in the classifier. One shared test helper reaching invalidated code dragged its
whole package along, and the report printed all of it — every file, with its own evidence block. The
verdicts were correct and the output was unusable, because 187 file names that all resolve to one
`go test ./internal/sem` bury the eight production files somebody actually has to open. The fix is not
to drop those files: a deleted result is a result nobody can audit. The fix is to rank them. Test
fallout collapses to one line per package carrying the command that checks it, production work stays
listed file by file with its evidence, and the JSON still carries all 636 files with their roles.

## Entire Graph findings and verification

Run against this repository at commit `934d180` — 634 files, of which the role classifier calls 277
PRODUCTION, 266 TEST and 91 TEST_FIXTURE:

| Run | INVALIDATED | AT-RISK | SAFE | UNREACHED | excluded |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--dependency net/http` | 3 | 78 | 468 | 85 | 0 |
| `--dependency net/http --exclude-tests` | **0** | **0** | 204 | 73 | 357 |
| `--dependency os/exec` | 32 | 287 | 230 | 85 | 0 |

- `internal/cli/pivot.go` — flags, graph load, the three classification rules, propagation, JSON.
- `internal/cli/pivot_roles.go` — file-role classification and the grouped text report.
- `internal/cli/pivot_plan.go` — the `pivot-plan/v1` work order.

```
entire graph pivot --dependency <prohibited package> [--checkpoint <id>] [--depth N]
                   [--exclude-tests] [--format text|json|plan]
```

Pipeline:

1. **Load the graph.** `sem.LoadOrBuildProviderSnapshot` — the same call `impact` uses, so pivot reuses
   the plugin's existing parse and cache rather than building a second index.
2. **Rule 1, direct conflict.** Any file with an `IMPORTS`, `CALLS`, or `CONSTRUCTS` edge reaching the
   prohibited dependency is **INVALIDATED**. This is checkpoint-independent by design: code written
   before Entire was ever enabled still violates a new constraint, and a classifier that could only see
   checkpointed files would silently clear all of it.
3. **Rule 2, propagation.** Breadth-first from the invalidated set over dependency edges. Anything
   reached is **AT-RISK**, recorded with its hop distance. Capped at 2 hops by default.
4. **Rule 3, the rest.** No path to anything invalidated means **SAFE** — but only for languages the
   graph parses semantically. Files in inventory-only languages are reported as **UNREACHED**, because
   calling a file safe when the parser never checked it for relations would be asserting an absence
   nobody verified.
5. **Checkpoint overlay (optional).** `sem.AnalyzeCheckpoint` folds in what a session changed and how
   many dependents each change has, and marks affected files that session wrote with `*`.
6. **Role pass.** Every file is classified **PRODUCTION | TEST | TEST_FIXTURE | GENERATED | VENDOR |
   UNKNOWN** from signals that cannot be argued with: a `vendor/` path segment, a
   `testdata|fixtures|mocks` segment, the `_test.go` suffix, or the `Code generated ... DO NOT EDIT.`
   header the generator itself wrote. The role never changes a verdict — it decides how the finished
   report is grouped and ranked.
7. **Render.** `text` for a person, `json` for the full classification, `plan` for an agent.

`--exclude-tests` (the same path predicate `impact` and `neighbors` use) drops test files *before*
classification rather than filtering them out of the finished report. The difference matters for
propagation, not just for the listing: a test file is not a foundation anything ships on, so a
production file whose only route to invalidated code runs through a test file should come back Safe,
not At-Risk. The count of excluded files is printed, because a file that was never classified is not
a file that came back Safe.

Every verdict prints the edge that produced it — relation type, target, confidence, source line — so a
reader can check the claim rather than trust it.

### Three design decisions worth defending

**The classifier is rules, not a model.** No LLM produces a verdict. The interpretive step — turning a
sentence like "we can't send customer data through Library X" into the package name `libraryx` — stays
outside this binary, and `--dependency` takes the result directly. That is not only a design
preference: `entire graph doctor` asserts `no_egress=true`, and a model call inside the plugin would
make the plugin's own diagnostic lie.

**Propagation is capped.** Unbounded transitive closure marks an entire repository At-Risk, which is
technically true and completely useless. Two hops, with the distance reported per file, keeps the
output a shortlist a person can actually work through.

**Roles rank the report; they never filter it.** The first version of this tool had a real usability
bug, and it was not in the classifier. One shared test helper reaching invalidated code dragged its
whole package along, and the report printed all of it — every file, with its own evidence block. The
verdicts were correct and the output was unusable, because 187 file names that all resolve to one

to drop those files: a deleted result is a result nobody can audit. The fix is to rank them. Test
fallout collapses to one line per package carrying the command that checks it, production work stays
listed file by file with its evidence, and the JSON still carries all 636 files with their roles.

## The work order: `--format plan`

The JSON report says what every file **is**. That is the right thing to archive and the wrong thing to
hand an agent, because an agent given a classification invents the plan itself — differently each
time, with no way afterwards to tell what it was supposed to have done. `--format plan` states the
work instead, as `pivot-plan/v1`.

Run at `--dependency os/exec --exclude-tests --depth 1` against `53ff6bd`: **278 work items — 8 P0,
11 P1, 259 P2**, with 7 required commands, 6 declared blind spots and 6 must-not-claim clauses.

The `plan_id` is deliberately not quoted here. It is a digest over the head commit, the constraint,
the depth, the flags and the counts, so it changes with every commit by design — that is what makes
two plans comparable or provably different. A fixed id printed in prose is stale the moment anything
lands, and a reader who cannot reproduce it has been given a number to distrust. Read it from the run
itself instead:

```sh
entire graph pivot --repo . --dependency os/exec --exclude-tests --depth 1 --format plan \
  | python3 -c "import sys,json; print(json.load(sys.stdin)['plan_id'])"
```

**Every classified file becomes exactly one work item**, so nothing falls between the report and the
plan: `INVALIDATED → REPLACE_OR_REMOVE`, `AT-RISK → VERIFY_AFTER_ROOT_FIX`, `SAFE → NO_ACTION`,
`UNREACHED → MANUAL_REVIEW`. Safe files are included deliberately: a file that was analysed and
cleared is a different thing from a file nobody looked at, and only the plan can tell an agent which
one it is holding.

**Priority encodes what blocks what.** P0 is a direct violation in code that ships — nothing
downstream can be verified until it is gone. P1 is a violation in a test, or shipped code standing on
an invalidated foundation. P2 is covered by running a package, or is not a change at all. Items are
sorted before ids are assigned, so reading the plan top to bottom is reading it in execution order.

**The plan id is deterministic** — a digest of head commit, constraint, depth, flags and counts — so
the same question asked twice is recognisably one plan rather than two.

Two parts of the schema exist because of how an *agent* fails rather than how the graph works:

- **`known_blind_spots`** pairs each limitation with its consequence, and is stated *before* the work
  items, because an agent decides how far to trust a plan before it reads it, not after. Six entries:
  interface dispatch, reflection, generated code, inventory-only languages, name matching, and that
  SAFE means no path was found in this snapshot rather than proof of absence.
- **`execution_contract.must_not_claim`** names the likely failure directly. It is not a bad edit — a
  test catches that. It is a confident report of success nobody ran a command to check. The clauses
  forbid claiming the dependency is gone without re-running pivot, claiming tests pass without
  executing them, treating SAFE as proof of absence, and counting an UNREACHED file as resolved. The
  GENERATED and VENDOR clauses appear only when those roles are actually present, so the contract
  stays signal rather than boilerplate.

`validation.required_commands` is where the package collapse becomes executable: `go build ./...`,
one `go test ./pkg` per affected package, and last the exact pivot re-run that proves the invalidated
count reached zero.

One correctness fix came out of building this. Propagation now carries the originating invalidated
file along the walk. At two hops an at-risk item used to report the intermediate neighbour it was
reached through; `root_invalidated` now names the file that actually has to be fixed first, which is
what the plan orders work by — `internal/cli/callsite.go` points at `internal/gitutil/git.go`, not at

`abbf061` and `4a0a219` carry no checkpoint, and that is worth stating rather than hiding. Entire's
hooks live in `.claude/settings.json` and load only when the agent session is launched from inside
that directory. Two earlier sessions were launched from the parent folder, never loaded the hooks,
and produced commits with no checkpoint attached — while `entire doctor` reported green throughout,
because it inspects the repository's settings file and cannot see where the agent was started from.

The failure is silent by construction, which is exactly the class of problem this project is about: a
tool reporting healthy is not the same as a tool having checked the thing you care about. The fix was
to verify the binding directly (`entire session current` naming a session, then `entire checkpoint
list` showing a non-zero count against a real commit) rather than trusting the diagnostic. Every
commit from `2ff8446` onward carries a checkpoint, verified that way.

## Setup, run and test instructions

```sh
mise run build          # builds ./entire-graph (needs Go + CGO for tree-sitter)
mise run test           # go test ./...

entire graph pivot --repo . --dependency net/http
entire graph pivot --repo . --dependency os/exec --exclude-tests --depth 1

entire graph pivot --repo . --dependency os/exec --exclude-tests --depth 1 --format plan
```

`mise run test` does not come back fully green on every machine: `cmd/graph-bench`'s clone helper
tests fail wherever the local git rejects `checkout --end-of-options`. Those failures reproduce at
`4a0a219`, before any of this work, and are unrelated to pivot — `internal/cli`, which is the only
package this feature touches, passes in full.

- **Static analysis cannot see dynamic dispatch.** A call through an interface, reflection, or
  generated code leaves no edge to follow, so a genuinely affected file can be reported Safe. This is a
  property of the underlying parser, not a bug in pivot, and it is the reason the report ends by saying
  Safe means "no path found," not "no path exists." Observed concretely: `impact --symbol Route.Match`
  on `gorilla/mux` reports 0 callers even though `Router.Match` calls it through an interface.
- **Constraint interpretation is out of scope by design.** Pivot takes a package name, not a sentence.
  The natural-language step belongs outside the no-egress boundary.
- **Prohibited-name matching is path-shaped** (exact, or a `pkg/` prefix). A dependency referred to by
  an alias in source is not currently resolved to its canonical package.
- **Test exclusion is path-shaped, not build-tag-shaped.** `--exclude-tests` recognizes conventional
  test paths (`_test.go`, `*.test.*`, a `test/`/`testdata/` directory segment, and the equivalents in
  the other supported languages). A test helper that lives in a normally-named file is still
  classified, and a production file that happens to sit under `testdata/` is still excluded.
- **Next step:** severity beyond the three buckets — an At-Risk file whose only link is a type
  reference is a much smaller job than one that calls an invalidated function on every request path,
  and the graph already carries enough to tell those apart.

but the reader now knows that eight of them are files to open and 24 are five commands to run. The
187 at-risk test files, which the previous version printed in full, are four lines:

```
TEST FALLOUT (187 file(s) across 4 package(s)) — collapsed on purpose.
These are covered by running the package, not by reading the list:
- internal/sem                        126 file(s)   go test ./internal/sem
- internal/cli                         58 file(s)   go test ./internal/cli
- internal/bench                        2 file(s)   go test ./internal/bench
- internal/sem/testdata/fixtures/typescript-http    1 file(s)   review internal/sem/testdata/fixtures/typescript-http/ (no Go test target derivable)
```

The last line is the honest case: a package with no Go in it is told so rather than handed a command
that would fail.

## The work order: `--format plan`

The JSON report says what every file **is**. That is the right thing to archive and the wrong thing to
hand an agent, because an agent given a classification invents the plan itself — differently each
time, with no way afterwards to tell what it was supposed to have done. `--format plan` states the
work instead, as `pivot-plan/v1`.

Run at `--dependency os/exec --exclude-tests --depth 1` against `53ff6bd`: **278 work items — 8 P0,
11 P1, 259 P2**, with 7 required commands, 6 declared blind spots and 6 must-not-claim clauses.

The `plan_id` is deliberately not quoted here. It is a digest over the head commit, the constraint,
the depth, the flags and the counts, so it changes with every commit by design — that is what makes
two plans comparable or provably different. A fixed id printed in prose is stale the moment anything
lands, and a reader who cannot reproduce it has been given a number to distrust. Read it from the run
itself instead:

```sh
entire graph pivot --repo . --dependency os/exec --exclude-tests --depth 1 --format plan \
  | python3 -c "import sys,json; print(json.load(sys.stdin)['plan_id'])"
```

**Every classified file becomes exactly one work item**, so nothing falls between the report and the
plan: `INVALIDATED → REPLACE_OR_REMOVE`, `AT-RISK → VERIFY_AFTER_ROOT_FIX`, `SAFE → NO_ACTION`,
`UNREACHED → MANUAL_REVIEW`. Safe files are included deliberately: a file that was analysed and
cleared is a different thing from a file nobody looked at, and only the plan can tell an agent which
one it is holding.

**Priority encodes what blocks what.** P0 is a direct violation in code that ships — nothing
downstream can be verified until it is gone. P1 is a violation in a test, or shipped code standing on
an invalidated foundation. P2 is covered by running a package, or is not a change at all. Items are
sorted before ids are assigned, so reading the plan top to bottom is reading it in execution order.

**The plan id is deterministic** — a digest of head commit, constraint, depth, flags and counts — so
the same question asked twice is recognisably one plan rather than two.

Two parts of the schema exist because of how an *agent* fails rather than how the graph works:

- **`known_blind_spots`** pairs each limitation with its consequence, and is stated *before* the work
  items, because an agent decides how far to trust a plan before it reads it, not after. Six entries:
  interface dispatch, reflection, generated code, inventory-only languages, name matching, and that
  SAFE means no path was found in this snapshot rather than proof of absence.
- **`execution_contract.must_not_claim`** names the likely failure directly. It is not a bad edit — a
  test catches that. It is a confident report of success nobody ran a command to check. The clauses
  forbid claiming the dependency is gone without re-running pivot, claiming tests pass without
  executing them, treating SAFE as proof of absence, and counting an UNREACHED file as resolved. The
  GENERATED and VENDOR clauses appear only when those roles are actually present, so the contract
  stays signal rather than boilerplate.

`validation.required_commands` is where the package collapse becomes executable: `go build ./...`,
one `go test ./pkg` per affected package, and last the exact pivot re-run that proves the invalidated
count reached zero.

One correctness fix came out of building this. Propagation now carries the originating invalidated
file along the walk. At two hops an at-risk item used to report the intermediate neighbour it was
reached through; `root_invalidated` now names the file that actually has to be fixed first, which is
what the plan orders work by — `internal/cli/callsite.go` points at `internal/gitutil/git.go`, not at
whatever it happened to be reached through.

## Checkpoint links and what each checkpoint proves

Every commit below is on `pivot-work-order`. `main` is protected on the Entire mirror, so the branch
lands via PR; the checkpoint ref (`entire/checkpoints/v1`) pushes independently of it.

| Checkpoint | Commit | Milestone | What it proves |
|---|---|---|---|
| — | `abbf061` | — | Classifier, propagation, evidence output. **No checkpoint** — see below. |
| — | `4a0a219` | — | `--exclude-tests` applied before classification. **No checkpoint** — see below. |
| `bb0d72d79dbc` | `2ff8446` | Initial understanding and architecture | Checkpoints bind from this worktree. The header keeps depth and index provenance on uncommitted runs, so a reader can tell how far propagation walked and whether the verdict came off a warm cache. |
| `4a14d2327199` | `934d180` | Last stable state before noon | File roles rank the report instead of listing it: 32 direct violations resolve to 8 production files to open by hand and 24 test files collapsed to 5 package commands. |

### The two commits with no checkpoint are the honest part

`abbf061` and `4a0a219` carry no checkpoint, and that is worth stating rather than hiding. Entire's
hooks live in `.claude/settings.json` and load only when the agent session is launched from inside
that directory. Two earlier sessions were launched from the parent folder, never loaded the hooks,
and produced commits with no checkpoint attached — while `entire doctor` reported green throughout,
because it inspects the repository's settings file and cannot see where the agent was started from.

The failure is silent by construction, which is exactly the class of problem this project is about: a
tool reporting healthy is not the same as a tool having checked the thing you care about. The fix was
to verify the binding directly (`entire session current` naming a session, then `entire checkpoint
list` showing a non-zero count against a real commit) rather than trusting the diagnostic. Every
commit from `2ff8446` onward carries a checkpoint, verified that way.

## Setup, run and test instructions

```sh
mise run build          # builds ./entire-graph (needs Go + CGO for tree-sitter)
mise run test           # go test ./...

entire graph pivot --repo . --dependency net/http
entire graph pivot --repo . --dependency os/exec --exclude-tests --depth 1
entire graph pivot --repo . --dependency net/http --checkpoint <id> --format json

# the agent work order
entire graph pivot --repo . --dependency os/exec --exclude-tests --depth 1 --format plan
```

`mise run test` does not come back fully green on every machine: `cmd/graph-bench`'s clone helper
tests fail wherever the local git rejects `checkout --end-of-options`. Those failures reproduce at
`4a0a219`, before any of this work, and are unrelated to pivot — `internal/cli`, which is the only
package this feature touches, passes in full.

## Known limitations and next steps

- **Static analysis cannot see dynamic dispatch.** A call through an interface, reflection, or
  generated code leaves no edge to follow, so a genuinely affected file can be reported Safe. This is a
  property of the underlying parser, not a bug in pivot, and it is the reason the report ends by saying
  Safe means "no path found," not "no path exists." Observed concretely: `impact --symbol Route.Match`
  on `gorilla/mux` reports 0 callers even though `Router.Match` calls it through an interface.
- **Constraint interpretation is out of scope by design.** Pivot takes a package name, not a sentence.
  The natural-language step belongs outside the no-egress boundary.
- **Prohibited-name matching is path-shaped** (exact, or a `pkg/` prefix). A dependency referred to by
  an alias in source is not currently resolved to its canonical package.
- **Test exclusion is path-shaped, not build-tag-shaped.** `--exclude-tests` recognizes conventional
  test paths (`_test.go`, `*.test.*`, a `test/`/`testdata/` directory segment, and the equivalents in
  the other supported languages). A test helper that lives in a normally-named file is still
  classified, and a production file that happens to sit under `testdata/` is still excluded.
- **Next step:** severity beyond the three buckets — an At-Risk file whose only link is a type
  reference is a much smaller job than one that calls an invalidated function on every request path,
  and the graph already carries enough to tell those apart.

Brief take, then I'll keep the graph work moving.

**Agreed, and it's cheap upside — but sequence matters.** The 15 graded points are the curveball adaptation; a big-repo run is what makes it *land* in the demo. So: clone now in the background (free), implement the tiers, then run the big repo through the *new* code. A big repo run through the old code proves nothing new.

**Which repo — pick for the thesis, not just size.** Our curveball claim is "the graph tiers its own uncertainty." The most impressive repo is one that produces all three tiers naturally:
- **Kubernetes** — biggest wow, heavy interface dispatch (exactly where the graph goes heuristic). Risk: parse time.
- **Prometheus** — big, pure Go, safe parse.
- **Grafana** — Go + TypeScript, so UNREACHED (inventory-only) lights up alongside Go tiers. Mixed-language is our strongest story.

Starting shallow clones now so parse cost overlaps the implementation.

content.text:
**Static analysis** = reading code without running it. It works when the answer is written down. These three hide the answer until runtime:

**Dynamic dispatch** — the code says "call `Handler.Serve()`" but `Handler` is an interface. Which actual function runs depends on what was plugged in at runtime. **Generated code** — a machine wrote the file, usually with a `DO NOT EDIT` header. It's real code that really runs, but nobody typed it, and it often isn't checked in. The parser may see nothing, or see thousands of files no human maintains.

**Reflection** — the code looks up a function *by its name as a string* at runtime: `reflect.ValueOf(x).MethodByName("Save")`. There is literally no call written in the source to follow. Grep for `Save` and you'd miss it too.

The common thread: **absence of an edge is not absence of a call.** That's exactly why our SAFE verdict says "no path found" and not "no path exists."

**Finding confirmed — and it's worse than the brief predicted.** Three facts from source:

1. **`Confidence` is captured but never consulted.** Set at `pivot.go:428` and `:476`; its *only* other appearance in the whole feature is `pivot_roles.go:409`, inside a `Fprintf`. It is printed and nothing else — never compared, never thresholded, never affects a verdict.
2. **`Resolution` is dropped entirely.** `sem.RelationRecord` carries `Resolution` ("exact" vs heuristic) and `WarningCodes` — `pivotEdge` copies **neither**. The graph's own statement of how it knows a fact never even enters PivotMap.
3. **The agent-facing plan has no confidence at all.** `grep` finds zero hits in `pivot_plan.go`. So a human sees an unusable number, and an agent — the audience most likely to act without checking — sees nothing.

And `Warnings` (`:348`) / `PartialFailures` (`:544`) are copied into the response and never read again. **SAFE genuinely conflates "parsed clean, no path" with "parser had diagnostics here, no path."**

9	// Evidence tiers separate what the graph proved from what it guessed.
10	//
11	// Before this existed, pivot carried each edge's confidence into the report and
12	// then never consulted it: the number was printed by writePivotFileLine and read
13	// by nothing. Two edges that mean very different things were rendered and treated
14	// identically, and a P0 work item could rest entirely on the weaker one with
15	// nothing saying so.
16	//
17	// The tiers are not a new opinion about the code. They are the graph's own
18	// resolution vocabulary, grouped by whether the relation was resolved to a
19	// declaration or inferred from a name.
20	const (
21		// evidenceConfirmed is a relation the parser resolved structurally: an import
22		// declaration it read, or a call it followed to a definition.
23		evidenceConfirmed = "CONFIRMED"
24		// evidenceHeuristic is a relation inferred rather than resolved -- matched by
25		// name, by package, or by an inferred receiver type. Often right, never proof.
26		evidenceHeuristic = "HEURISTIC"
27		// evidenceUnverified is a relation whose file the parser could not fully read.
28		// The edge may be right; the absence of other edges in that file is unknown,
29		// which is the part that makes a Safe verdict unsafe.
30		evidenceUnverified = "UNVERIFIED"
31	)
32	
33	// confirmedResolutions are the graph's words for "I followed this to a
34	// declaration" as opposed to "I matched a name".
35	//
36	// Measured on this repository (57,791 relations), the resolution vocabulary and
37	// the confidence attached to each is:
38	//
39	//	CALLS      import_external  0.78   8250   inferred: call attributed via an import
40	//	CALLS      exact            0.92   7248   resolved: followed to a definition
41	//	CALLS      package          0.80   5548   inferred: package-level attribution
42	//	IMPORTS    name_only        0.80   2170   an import declaration read from source
43	//	CALLS      name_only        0.68    761   inferred: globally unique method name
44	//	CALLS      import_resolved  0.84    254   resolved through an import path
45	//	CALLS      type_inferred    0.90    208   inferred from a receiver type
46	//	IMPORTS    import_resolved  0.93    146   resolved: import declaration + target
47	//	CALLS      pattern          0.70    123   inferred from a framework pattern
48	//
49	// Two things fall out of that table, and both shaped these rules.
50	//
51	// First, confidence alone cannot carry the distinction. 0.80 covers both
52	// `IMPORTS name_only` -- an import statement physically present in the source --
53	// and `CALLS package`, which is a guess about which package a call landed in.
54	// A threshold over confidence would put a fact and an inference in the same tier.
55	// Resolution is the axis that separates them, so the tiers key on resolution and
56	// use confidence only as a floor.
57	//
58	// Second, no relation in this repository carries confidence 1.00. The highest is
59	// 0.95. Any design that waited for certainty would tier everything as uncertain.
60	var confirmedResolutions = map[string]bool{
61		"exact":           true,
62		"import_resolved": true,
63		"full":            true,
64		"resolved":        true,
65		"signature":       true,
66	}
67	
68	// confirmedByRelation are relation types that are read directly out of the source
69	// text rather than inferred, whatever the parser managed to resolve the target to.
70	//
71	// IMPORTS is here because of the 2,170 `IMPORTS name_only` edges above. The
72	// `name_only` describes the target: the parser did not bind the imported package
73	// to a symbol it had parsed. It does not describe the import statement, which was
74	// read from the file. For a prohibited-dependency question that statement is the
75	// strongest evidence there is -- it is the line a reviewer would grep for -- so
76	// grading it HEURISTIC because the far end went unresolved would understate it.
77	var confirmedByRelation = map[string]bool{
78		"IMPORTS": true,
79	}
80	
81	// confirmedConfidenceFloor is a floor, not a threshold. Resolution decides the
82	// tier; this only stops an edge the parser resolved but then flagged as weak from
83	// being presented as confirmed. Set below the 0.84 of `CALLS import_resolved` so
84	// it does not silently demote a whole resolution class.
85	const confirmedConfidenceFloor = 0.80
86	
87	// classifyEvidenceTier grades one edge. incompleteFiles are the files the parser
88	// reported a warning or partial failure against; an edge attached to one of those
89	// is UNVERIFIED regardless of how well it resolved, because the problem is not
90	// that edge but the edges that may be missing beside it.
91	func classifyEvidenceTier(relationType, resolution string, confidence float64, warningCodes []string, filePath string, incompleteFiles map[string]string) string {
92		if len(warningCodes) > 0 {
93			return evidenceUnverified
94		}
95		if _, incomplete := incompleteFiles[filePath]; incomplete {
96			return evidenceUnverified
97		}
98		if confirmedByRelation[relationType] {
99			return evidenceConfirmed
100		}
101		if confirmedResolutions[resolution] && confidence >= confirmedConfidenceFloor {
102			return evidenceConfirmed
103		}
104		return evidenceHeuristic
105	}
106	
107	// tierRank orders the tiers weakest-last so a file can be summarised by its worst
108	// piece of evidence. A verdict is only as good as the shakiest edge holding it up.
109	func tierRank(tier string) int {
110		switch tier {
111		case evidenceConfirmed:
112			return 0
113		case evidenceHeuristic:
114			return 1
115		case evidenceUnverified:
116			return 2
117		default:
118			return 1
119		}
120	}
121	
122	// weakestEvidenceTier summarises a file's evidence by its weakest edge. A file
123	// held up by one confirmed import and one name-matched call is reported at the
124	// name-matched end, because that is the claim a reader has to check.
125	//
126	// A file with no evidence at all -- Safe, or Unreached -- returns "", and the
127	// caller decides what that means. Safe with no evidence is not weak evidence; it
128	// is the absence of a path, which the verdict already says.
129	func weakestEvidenceTier(evidence []pivotEdge) string {
130		weakest := ""
131		for _, edge := range evidence {
132			if weakest == "" || tierRank(edge.Tier) > tierRank(weakest) {
133				weakest = edge.Tier
134			}
135		}
136		return weakest
137	}
138	
139	// incompleteAnalysisFiles collects every file the parser could not fully read,
140	// mapped to the reason it gave. Both header channels feed it: PartialFailures
141	// names files that failed outright, Warnings names files that parsed with a
142	// caveat. Pivot copied both into its response before this change and consulted
143	// neither, which is what let a file with a broken parse be reported Safe.
144	func incompleteAnalysisFiles(header sem.SnapshotHeader) map[string]string {
145		incomplete := make(map[string]string)
146		for _, failure := range header.PartialFailures {
147			if failure.FilePath == "" {
148				continue
149			}
150			incomplete[failure.FilePath] = failure.Code
151		}
152		for _, warning := range header.Warnings {
153			if warning.FilePath == "" {
154				continue
155			}
156			if _, exists := incomplete[warning.FilePath]; !exists {
157				incomplete[warning.FilePath] = warning.Code
158			}
159		}
160		return incomplete
161	}
162	
163	// sortedIncompleteFiles renders the set deterministically for the report.
164	func sortedIncompleteFiles(incomplete map[string]string) []string {
165		paths := make([]string, 0, len(incomplete))
166		for path := range incomplete {
167			paths = append(paths, path)
168		}
169		sort.Strings(paths)
170		return paths
171	}

**That's the money shot, and it's real — not a fixture.**

Five files in our own repo were reported **SAFE** before this change:

```
internal/sem/grammars/csharp/tree_sitter/array.h    E_PARSE_ERROR

```

PivotMap used to say *"SAFE — no dependency path to invalidated code, leave alone."* The parser had **failed to read those files at all**. The old report presented a parse failure as a clean bill of health, in the exact words the card forbids. It now says UNVERIFIED and names the parser's own error code.

And the CONFIRMED/HEURISTIC split lands where it should:
- `callsite.go → git.go` — `import_resolved` → **CONFIRMED**, no verify line
- `preflight.go → verify.go` — `package` → **HEURISTIC** → *"VERIFY: confirm in source or by test"*

Same repo, same command, both tiers, self-demonstrating. Now the agent-facing plan.
